seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Pound: That lady should apply for leave to Jonathan Cape. Between ourselves, Italian writers and editors for the last 6 or 7 years have been publishing translations of my stories but they never had the courtesy to send me a copy of the paper or to pay a sou
.
I send you an article about Lucia’s lettrines . They are very beautiful though a half-blind father is no good judge. Lord knows where she got the talent. Not from me.

We are here flat hunting. I hope you like my new poetical address. Enclosed please find a picture of my grandson, Stephen James , snapped at Cap Ferrat a few weeks ago. I hope your son and heir is thriving. Two Japanese firms have pirated Ulysses
. This work is now coming out in the Albatross Press.
My sight is very slightly better but I have to go to Zurich every 3 months for inspection. A great pity I did not meet Prof. Vogt eight years ago.
I hope you are in better shape than your namesake Mr Sterling. What does he mean by going off the key like that when I have so many bills to pay?

postscript.p: P.S. The British Customs seized Lucia’s book because the carton was silk!

div.note: The Hotel Lord Byron, near the Place de l’Étoile (now Place Charles de Gaulle), was described in a 1924 guidebook as “100 beds, P[ension, i.e., board, lodging, and attendance]. from 35 fr[ancs]” (Karl Baedeker, Paris and its Environs [Leipzig: Karl Baedeker, 1924], 7).

Uncertain. At least two women were translating JJ’s Dubliners stories into Italian around this time. Annie Lami, with Adriano Lami, published a translation, titled Gente di Dublino, with Edizioni Corbaccio in Milan in March 1933. Also, Amalia Risolo translated five of the stories and published them under the title Araby with the firm of Carlo Moscheni in Trieste in 1935. Risolo was the married name of Amalia Popper (1891-1967), whom JJ tutored in English in Trieste around 1908-1909 and who, some scholars believe, might have been one of the inspirations for the brooding, erotic epiphanies that he wrote circa 1911-1914 and that are collected in Giacomo Joyce (London: Faber and Faber; New York: Viking Press, 1968). (For discussion of Popper, see John McCourt, The Years of Bloom: James Joyce in Trieste 1904-1920 [Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 2000], 199-204.)

The publisher Jonathan Cape, Ltd., of London, acquired from the Egoist Press in 1924 the rights to JJ’s Chamber Music, Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and Exiles. Herbert Jonathan Cape (1879-1960) founded the firm with Wren Howard in 1921, going on to publish works by H.G. Wells, W.H. Davies, Sinclair Lewis, Ernest Hemingway, Margaret Mead, and other authors. For additional details, see Nora Joyce to Pound, 22 February 1931, notes; 17 August 1932, notes.
JJ’s complaints about unauthorized and unremunerative Italian translations of his writings had become a point of contention with Pound several months before. See JJ to Pound, 29 February 1932, notes.

note.p: The first English edition (printed in France) of JJ’s Pomes Penyeach was published in September or October 1932 by Desmond Harmsworth Ltd. in London and The Obelisk Press in Paris. The poems were rendered in facsimile of JJ’s handwriting, with the poems’ initial letters (or lettrines) designed by JJ’s daughter, Lucia (1907-1982). The handsome volume was printed on Japanese nacre paper in an edition of 25 copies, enclosed in a portfolio of green watered silk, with the front cover gilt stamped in facsimile of JJ’s handwriting. Copies sold for 1,000 francs each (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 38-39). JJ, who was finding ways of paying Lucia for her artwork in order to boost her confidence, arranged to take no royalties on this edition and to have her paid 33% of the net profits (LIII 266). Pomes Penyeach, containing thirteen poems by JJ, had initially been published in 1927 by Shakespeare and Company in Paris.

The “article” JJ mentions could have been a notice or statement by the French art historian and writer, Louis Gillet (1876-1943), the Belgian art critic and author, Fritz Vanderpyl (1876-1965), or another source. Shloss discusses early reviews and notices of Lucia’s lettrines, as well as “interviews occasioned by the publication of Lucia’s work” (Carol Loeb Shloss, Lucia Joyce: To Dance in the Wake [New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2003], 243-46). Vanderpyl’s “Pulchritudo tam Antiqua et tam Nova: Les Lettrines de Lucia Joyce” appeared in transition, no. 22 (February 1933): 131. Gillet wrote JJ around June 1932: “J’admire ces lettrines comme une merveille d’atavisme. On dirait des caprices d’un vieil enlumineur irlandais. La T surtout est étonnante. … J’ai peur que nos artistes aient peu de chose à apprendre à cette jeune fille que guide la main de Saint Patrice ou Saint Colomban” (“I admire these lettrines as a marvel of atavism. One might call them the fancies of an old Irish illuminator. The ‘T’ especially is astonishing. I fear that our artists have little to teach this girl who is guided by the hand of St. Patrick or St. Columbanus”) (LI 319). Gillet wrote a preface to A Chaucer A.B.C., which featured illuminated initial letters by Lucia and was published by The Obelisk Press in Paris in 1936.

div.note: JJ, Nora, and Lucia stayed at the Hotel Lord Bryon from 20 October to 28 November 1932 until they found a furnished flat at 42 rue Galilée in Paris, where they remained until July 1934.

The Hotel Lord Byron. As a schoolboy, JJ had defended the literary merits of the English poet George Gordon, Lord Byron (1788-1824), against his fellows’ claims that Byron was immoral and a heretic (Ellmann, JJ 39-40) – a scene that JJ recreated in A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (P 80-82). JJ tried to persuade the American composer George Antheil (1900-1959) – and later the Swiss composer Othmar Schoeck (1886-1957) – to write an opera based on Lord Byron’s closet drama Cain: A Mystery (1821), as a vehicle for JJ’s favorite tenor, John O’Sullivan, or Sullivan (1877-1955). Neither did so.

note.p: Stephen James Joyce (1932-2020) was born in France, the son of JJ’s son, Giorgio (1905-1976), and his wife, Helen Kastor Fleischman Joyce (1894-1963). Stephen graduated from Harvard University and later worked for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), with an emphasis on African development. On retiring from the OECD in 1991, he turned his attention to managing JJ’s literary estate and trust, and became notorious for his hostility to most forms of Joyce scholarship and for his use of his grandfather’s copyrights to enforce his views and sometimes to demand high permissions fees. He and his wife, Solange Raythchine Joyce (d. 2016), lived in France and had no children (see obituary, New York Times, [8 February 2020]).

Stephen was born shortly after JJ’s father, John Stanislaus Joyce (1849-1931), died. In his combined grief and joy, JJ wrote a moving poem, “Ecce Puer” (CP 63). As a young boy, Stephen spent time with JJ, who showed him great affection and told and wrote him charming stories, two of which are preserved in letters he wrote in 1936 (see LI 386-87 for one of these). These letter-tales have been published as The Cat and the Devil (New York: Dodd, Mead and Company, 1964) andThe Cats of Copenhagen (New York: Scribner, 2012). Several photographs show JJ and his young grandson Stephen together in family settings.

div.note: Giorgio Joyce, his wife Helen, and their son Stephen were at La Ferme du May, Saint Jean-Cap Ferrat, Alpes Maritimes, France, during the summer of 1932, where they were visited by Helen’s family (LIII 249).

Omar Shakespear Pound (1926-2010), the son of Dorothy Shakespear Pound (1886-1973), was born in France and cared for in England by his maternal grandmother, Olivia Shakespear (1863-1938), and by the Norland Institute and a former matron of Norland. He attended Charterhouse School, survived the London Blitz, and served as a volunteer in the U.S. Army during World War II. Pound later attended Hamilton College in New York–Ezra Pound’s alma mater–and also studied at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London, and McGill University in Montreal. A scholar of Arabic and Persian literatures, Pound became a noted translator of poetry in those languages, as well as a poet, in English, in his own right. Later in life, he lived and taught in Princeton, New Jersey, and published numerous scholarly articles and volumes on Ezra Pound and Wyndham Lewis.

A Japanese translation of Ulysses, by Tadashi Ito and others, was published in two volumes in Tokyo in 1931 and 1934. Another, by Sohei Morita and others, appeared in five volumes in Tokyo from 1932 to 1935 (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 123). JJ wrote T.S. Eliot in June 1932: “Two Japanese pirated editions of Ulysses have appeared this spring and 13,000 copies have been sold to date. Is Japan a signatory to the Berne convention or not. Ulysses stands under French law. The pirates allege that European books become public property in Japan after 10 years” (LI 320). Later in 1932, JJ reported that “[t]he Japanese sent me a cheque for 200 yen (£10, circa) for their depredations. I am sending it back with a Chinese curse on it and them” (LI 325). JJ was not mollified when he was informed that Ulysses was not protected under the short Japanese copyright term for European works (see Robert Spoo, Without Copyrights: Piracy, Publishing, and the Public Domain [New York: Oxford University Press, 2013], 237, 319 n.23). He was uninterested in any distinction between legality and morality when it came to unauthorized uses of his writings. JJ’s commentators, no less than JJ himself, have sometimes been guilty of casual accusations of “piracy” even when they have known that JJ’s works lacked copyright protection (see, e.g., Ellmann, JJ 654-55 & n.; LI 325 n.1).

note.p: Ellmann writes: “J. Holroyd-Reece and M.C. Wegner, the Paris representatives of the Albatross Press, with headquarters in Hamburg, offered to take over the publication of Ulysses, and Joyce signed with them a contract that allocated 25% of the royalties to Sylvia Beach for five years and 7½% for life” (Ellmann, JJ 652-53). This edition, issued under the special imprint of The Odyssey Press, and printed in Germany, was published in Hamburg in December 1932 in two volumes and in a one-volume paper edition. The edition benefited from revisions by JJ’s friend, the English scholar and translator Stuart Gilbert (1883-1969), and was long considered “the most accurate and authoritative text of Ulysses” (Slocum and Cahoon, 29-30).

In December 1933, JJ’s friend and secretary Paul Léon (1893-1942) wrote letters to Holroyd-Reece and Wegner, expressing alarm that they were planning to import their Ulysses edition into the United States so as to compete with the imminent Random House edition (1934) there. The two publishers protested that they had been misunderstood, but in fact they had made (and withdrawn) a proposal that could be construed as an attempt to exploit the questionable U.S. copyright in Ulysses. JJ’s eyesight was remarkably good when it came to spotting pirate flags on the horizon (see Spoo, Without Copyrights, 248-51).

div.note: In July 1932, JJ went to Zurich to consult the noted eye surgeon, Professor Alfred Vogt (1879-1943). Vogt upbraided him for not having come earlier, and felt that his right eye was close to irreparable blindness. He proposed two operations, followed by surgery on the left eye. JJ wrote a correspondent in November 1932: “I went to Zurich in July and Professor Vogt (probably the greatest eye-doctor in the world) found that my sight had somewhat improved. I have to return to him every three months for a year or a year and a half to be under constant observation. He is afraid to touch the bad eye until the process of amelioration in the other has reached its highest point. As these wretched eyes of mine have already been operated on ten times (unfortunately not by him, except the last time) after about 25 years of recurrent inflamations [sic] it is a very delicate case to handle” (LIII 266-67).

note.p: The British pound was fluctuating against foreign currencies throughout 1932. For example, in November 1932, the pound reached roughly $3.20 against the U.S. dollar, its lowest point since 1920 (“British Pound Reacts to Lowest Level Since ’20 Due to Debt Terms,” Binghamton Press, New York [25 November 1932]: 1). Though the pound was gaining again by the end of November, instability in the payment of war debt kept the markets volatile.

“Mr Sterling” was an old joke between JJ and Pound. When they were younger, JJ’s children called Pound “Signore Sterlina” – a homophonic coincidence of his name with the British pound sterling – partly because they had come to associate him, as JJ himself had, with financial relief, especially prior to 1920 (see JJ to Pound, 5 December 1918, notes).

div.note: There may be an allusion here to Georgina Ann Stirling (ca. 1866-1935), a noted Newfoundland opera soprano, known by her stage name Marie Toulinquet, who sang in opera houses throughout Europe and United States. She was hailed as The Nightingale of the North.

Copies of JJ’s Pomes Penyeach, printed with initial letters (or lettrines) designed by JJ’s daughter, Lucia, and sold in special silk casings (see note 5, above), were seized at British Customs. JJ wrote another correspondent: “the British Customs seized the whole 10 copies (9 sold in advance) of the English part of my daughter’s book of lettrines on account of the ‘carton’ classing it as ‘silk luxury goods’ and demanding a Chinese ransom of £4 per copy on a book which already costs £12 a copy. No wonder the £ is at 82 in the shade” (LIII 265).
